issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Grief Reminders' is not well aligned with the indexed trauma of witnessing domestic violence in childhood unless there was also a salient bereavement/loss component. None of the other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal items indicate traumatic loss, so this strategy appears to target a different problem domain than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is hard to reconcile with this patient's age (21), single status, and the rest of the profile unless a specific caretaking or protective role is central to the trauma narrative. The other items emphasize danger sensitivity, helpless coping, and injustice toward perpetrators, but do not support a salient role-failure theme, making this appraisal feel insufficiently grounded in the profile.

vignette: María, a 21-year-old animator from a Latino family, first noticed the echo of a childhood nightmare when a client in her studio laughed loudly at a badly rendered character. The sudden burst of laughter, a sharp clatter that reminded her of the day her father had slammed a chair into a shelf, sent a ripple of dread through her. The sound, a trigger, instantly pulled her into a defensive stance. She reached for her phone to draft a new storyline, but her hand trembled and she abandoned the script, deciding that if she were to think about future projects, the world might collapse again. The same day, a colleague's comment about "throwing in extra lines" triggered the memory of a toy that had been hurled by her brother's friend into the living room. The object-throwing image was so vivid that María felt as if the scene played out in real time; the memory of the event leapt out of her mind more intensely than ordinary recollections. In that instant, her mind made the leap from trigger to threat: she felt a sudden startle, her heart pounding, as if the living room still existed and someone could throw a chair at her again. The same moment also prompted a maladaptive strategy: she closed the laptop, turned off the lights, and fled to her bedroom, convinced that planning ahead could invite catastrophe. The chain of events-trigger sparking maladaptive strategy, threat, and memory-sent her spiraling deeper into the night of her past. The more María revisited that vivid scene-images of her mother's face, the sharp metallic scent of a broken mug, the echo of slammed furniture-the more she pushed the memory away before it could fully settle, as if her mind were a safety valve. The blocked memory fed her avoidance of future plans: she avoided drawing timelines or brainstorming ideas for months, believing that setting goals made her vulnerable to a repeat of that violent scene. The same blockage also intensified her hypervigilance; she was constantly scanning for any sign of an impending threat, a reflex that grew from the intensity of the memory. As she stayed on guard, she began to think that she could never cope with even the slightest upset, reinforcing a negative appraisal of her own resilience. The memory's grip also made her feel that the people responsible had faced no consequences, deepening her sense of helplessness. Each time she avoided planning, the memory seemed fresher, a vicious loop that tightened her self-perception of helplessness. When María felt a sudden jolt in the studio-an elevator door sliding shut with a loud thud-she reacted as though danger hovered. The threat she perceived triggered her avoidance behaviors: she left the studio abruptly, even though the elevator was just a mechanical mishap. Her startle reflex also pulled the memory back to the forefront, a sudden flash of her father's fists and the sound of glass cracking. The presence of a threat seemed to bring the past to her present, forcing her to replay the memory even as she tried to escape it. In that moment, her internal world felt like a repeating loop: threat leads to avoidance, avoidance triggers memory, memory strengthens threat. The avoidance that María engaged in-abandoning future planning, restricting her meals to a strict regimen of counting calories, steering clear of anything that reminded her of her father-began to alter her perception of reality. When she ate only the measured portions she felt she could regain some control over her body, a strategy that felt necessary to keep her from feeling as if she were again at the mercy of an unpredictable world. But this strategy only cemented the memory of the day when she was forced to keep a watchful eye on her own heartbeat, feeling it as a relentless metronome that counted down to the next violent event. The more she avoided planning, the more she believed that her future could never be safe, reinforcing her negative appraisal that she could not cope. Her hypervigilant state persisted; she remained on guard not only against external threats but also against the possibility that the memory would surge unexpectedly. The loop of maladaptive strategy, threat, memory, and negative appraisal grew tighter each day, eroding her ability to engage in work or social interactions. Now, after months of isolation and a steady decline in her creative output, María finally reached out for help. The last week, she missed a deadline and received an email from her supervisor reminding her that she was one of the most talented animators on the team. The disappointment, coupled with the lingering fear that she could not manage even a small setback, pushed her over the edge. She now fears that her memories will continue to haunt her, that she will never find a safe space to plan or create, yet she also hopes that learning to manage her triggers might restore her confidence in her craft and her ability to envision a future that does not echo the past.
